Role of CanIf: hardware-independent hub between CAN drivers and communication stack

The CAN Interface (CanIf) takes over all hardware-independent tasks of CAN communication of an ECU. The underlying CAN drivers thus only deal with access to and control of the respective CAN hardware. CanIf processes transmit requests, transmit confirmations, receive and error indications as well as start and stop of the CAN controllers. Its data APIs operate on CAN L-SDUs, its control APIs are related to the CAN controller (⟦0⟧). CanIf never accesses hardware-specific communication buffers directly, but exclusively via services of the CanDrv ⟦1⟧.

Downwards, CanIf serves one or more CanDrv. In link-time configuration, this is done via a set of function pointers per driver ⟦0⟧. In addition, CanIf combines the APIs of multiple CanTrcv into a uniform interface without containing transceiver logic itself (⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧). Upwards, there are configurable users:
PduR, CanNm, CanTp, Xcp, and CDDs as data users (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧),
CanSM as control instance for controller and transceiver modes ⟦0⟧,
EcuM for initialization and wake-up (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧).

It fragments I-PDUs that do not fit into an assigned FlexRay L-PDU into segments and reassembles them upon reception (⟦0⟧). Transmission types according to ISO 10681-2
FrTp supports six transfer types:
unsegmented, without and with acknowledgment, with known length (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧);
segmented, without and with acknowledgment, with known length (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧);
segmented, without and with acknowledgment, with unknown length (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧).

A segmented transfer consists of StartFrame, FlowControl, ConsecutiveFrames, and LastFrame. A ConsecutiveFrame_EOB terminates a block; thereafter, the receiver enables the next block via FlowControl (⟦0⟧).
Transfers with unknown length work as follows:
The function is enabled via compiler switch (⟦0⟧).
The upper layer requests it with ⟦0⟧ (⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧).
The transfer ends as soon as the upper layer reports length 0 (⟦0⟧).
FrTp sums the partial lengths and transmits the total length in the LastFrame (⟦0⟧).
On 1:n connections, there is neither acknowledgment nor retry (⟦0⟧). Segmentation leads to error ⟦1⟧ there (⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧).

Each transmit operation begins with ⟦0⟧ (⟦1⟧). The service sets ⟦2⟧ only if the TxPduId is valid and a channel is available (⟦3⟧). Otherwise, it returns ⟦4⟧ (⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧). The same applies if a transfer is already running for the same address information (⟦7⟧). The addresses originate from ⟦8⟧/⟦9⟧ or from the metadata ⟦10⟧/⟦11⟧ (⟦12⟧, ⟦13⟧).
In the MainFunction, the transmit operation proceeds in these steps:
FrTp determines the available length via ⟦0⟧ (⟦1⟧).
FrTp allocates the first free FrTpTxPdu of the pool (⟦0⟧). If none is available, the connection is postponed to the next call (⟦1⟧).
Based on the length of this PDU, FrTp decides whether segmentation is required (⟦0⟧).
FrTp copies payload in PDU length (⟦0⟧) and sends it with ⟦1⟧ and exact length (⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧).
⟦0⟧ confirms each N-PDU and resets the FrTpTxPdu to “idle” (⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧).
If ⟦0⟧ returns ⟦1⟧, FrTp retries up to FrTpTimeCs times (⟦2⟧).

Channel and flag are released as soon as three conditions are met: all data has been transmitted, the confirmation is positive, and in case of acknowledgment, the final acknowledgment has arrived (⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧). For each accepted request, FrTp calls ⟦2⟧ exactly once, with ⟦3⟧ or ⟦4⟧ (⟦5⟧).

For the transmit direction, there are two buffer modes, “Immediate” and “Decoupled Buffer Access” (⟦0⟧). In decoupled mode, the lower layer fetches the N-PDU via ⟦1⟧. In doing so, FrTp copies address information, PCI, and data with exact length (⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧). Since this call runs in interrupt context, AI and PCI should be locally buffered in advance (⟦4⟧).
